title: Google Maps
seoTitle: Design Google Maps — Map Tiles, Routing and Live Traffic
description: Design Google Maps — serving map tiles through CDNs, place search, fast routing on a road graph with precomputation, live traffic from phone location data, and ETA prediction.
author: Editorial Team

blocks.title: What is Google Maps?
blocks.text: Google Maps shows an interactive map of the world, finds places, and gives directions with travel times that account for live traffic. It's really three systems: a **map rendering** system (tiles), a **search** system for places and addresses, and a **routing** system that finds the fastest path on a road network of hundreds of millions of segments, using traffic data collected from phones.

items: Users should be able to view and pan/zoom a map of any area.
Users should be able to search for places and addresses.
Users should get a route between two points with an ETA, for driving (and walking/cycling).
ETAs and routes should reflect current traffic, and navigation should reroute when conditions change.
Street View and satellite imagery capture.

blocks.question: What are the non-functional requirements for this system?

items: Map panning is smooth: tiles load in < 100 ms.
Routes computed in < 1 second, even across a continent.
Traffic reflects reality within a couple of minutes.
Scale to ~1B monthly users, millions of route requests per minute, and location updates from hundreds of millions of devices.
Accurate ETAs (within ~10% most of the time).
**Tile**: a square image or vector data for zoom level z and coordinates (x, y).
**Road graph**: nodes (intersections) and edges (road segments) with length, speed limit, restrictions.
**Traffic speed**: current average speed per road segment, with timestamp.
**Location ping**: anonymised device position and speed, used to derive traffic.

blocks.code:
GET  /tiles/{z}/{x}/{y}.pbf            (via CDN, vector tiles)
GET  /search?q=&near=lat,lng
GET  /directions?from=&to=&mode=driving&depart=now -> { routes: [{ polyline, eta, steps }] }
POST /navigation/:sessionId/location { lat, lng, speed }   (during navigation)

blocks.text: The world is divided into **tiles** at each zoom level (a quadtree: level z has 4^z tiles). Tiles are pre-generated from map data as **vector tiles** (roads, labels, shapes) that the client renders, so one tile works at any screen resolution and style. Tiles are static and served from a **CDN**, with clients caching them heavily.

Places and addresses are indexed in a search system with text fields and a **geo field**, so queries rank by text match, popularity and distance from the user or viewport. Address queries use a **geocoder** that parses the address and finds the matching point.

The **Routing Service** loads the road graph into memory. A plain Dijkstra search across a continent explores millions of nodes and takes too long, so the graph is **preprocessed** (see deep dive) to answer queries in milliseconds. Edge weights are travel times from the current traffic data.

Phones with location sharing send anonymised speed and position. A streaming pipeline **map-matches** each ping to a road segment and computes current average speed per segment over the last few minutes. Speeds update the routing weights and the traffic colours on map tiles (as a separate overlay layer, refreshed every minute).
1) How do we compute routes in milliseconds?

approach.text: Run Dijkstra from origin to destination over the whole road network.

challenges.text: A cross-country route explores tens of millions of nodes — seconds of CPU per request.

approach.text: Use A* with a distance heuristic and split the map into regions, searching only regions between origin and destination.

challenges.text: Faster, but long routes still explore huge areas, and traffic changes require care.

approach.text: Preprocess the graph into a hierarchy: **contraction hierarchies** add shortcut edges so a query only climbs to "important" roads and back down, exploring a few thousand nodes. For live traffic, use **customisable route planning (CRP)**: the graph is partitioned into cells once, and only the cheap "customisation" step (recomputing shortcut costs inside cells) runs when traffic weights change — every minute or so. Queries then take milliseconds.

challenges.text: Preprocessing is heavy and memory-hungry; graph data is replicated across many routing servers per region.

blocks.text: 2) How do we turn location pings into traffic?

Hundreds of millions of devices send pings, partitioned by **region/tile** in Kafka. A stream processor map-matches pings to segments (using a hidden Markov model over the road graph), filters outliers (a parked car, a cyclist on a road), and aggregates speeds per segment per minute, requiring a minimum number of devices for privacy. Segments without live data fall back to **historical speed profiles** for that time of week.
Mention that ETA isn't just sum of current speeds: traffic will change during a long trip, so an ETA model predicts future segment speeds from historical patterns plus current conditions.
3) How do we serve tiles at this scale?

There are trillions of possible tiles, but traffic is extremely skewed toward cities and common zoom levels. Pre-render popular tiles; generate rare ones **on demand** and cache them. Vector tiles are small and compress well; the CDN handles almost all requests, and clients cache tiles locally (also enabling **offline maps** by downloading a region's tiles and graph).

quiz.question: Why are map tiles served from a CDN?
options: Tiles are static and heavily reused, so edge caching handles almost all requests
quiz.explanation: Tiles change rarely and are requested enormously often.

quiz.question: Why isn't plain Dijkstra used for long routes?
options: It explores far too many nodes for millisecond responses
quiz.explanation: Preprocessed hierarchies make queries orders of magnitude faster.

quiz.question: What does customisable route planning make cheap?
options: Updating route weights when traffic changes
quiz.explanation: Only the customisation step reruns, not full preprocessing.

quiz.question: What is map-matching?
options: Assigning noisy GPS pings to the road segment the device is actually on
quiz.explanation: It's the first step in turning pings into segment speeds.
